title: Ἀνὴρ δειλὸς καὶ κόρακες
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 47. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A cowardly man was going out to war.
sentences.n: ἐξῄει is the imperfect of ἔξειμι, 'go out': it sets him on the road without getting him there. The same verb returns in the next sentence, when he sets out a second time.

sentences.t: Φθεγξαμένων δὲ κοράκων, τὰ ὅπλα θεὶς ἡσύχαζεν, εἶτ’ ἀναλαβὼν αὖθις ἐξῄει, καὶ φθεγγομένων πάλιν, ὑπέστη καὶ τέλος εἶπεν· « Ὑμεῖς κεκράξεσθε μὲν ὡς δύνασθε μέγιστον· ἐμοῦ δὲ οὐ γεύσεσθε. »
sentences.tr: Phthenxamenōn de korakōn, ta hopla theis hēsychazen, eit' analabōn authis exēiei, kai phthengomenōn palin, hypestē kai telos eipen· « Hymeis kekraxesthe men hōs dynasthe megiston· emou de ou geusesthe. »
sentences.l: And ravens having-cried-out, having-laid-down his arms he kept quiet; then having-taken-them-up he was going out again, and they crying once more, he came to a stand and at last said: « You will screech, indeed, as loudly as you can — but of me you shall not taste. »
sentences.i: Some ravens croaked, and he laid down his weapons and kept still; then he took them up and set out again, and when they croaked once more he stopped, and at last said: « Screech away as loud as you can — you shall not taste me. »
sentences.n: Ravens are birds of omen and the carrion birds of a battlefield: their cry both foretells his death and lays claim to his body, which is why he answers them as though they were already at the meal. Two genitive absolutes, aorist then present (φθεγξαμένων … φθεγγομένων): they cried out once, then were crying on. κεκράξεσθε is a future perfect of κράζω serving as a plain future. ὑπέστη, aorist of ὑφίστημι, is taken here as 'came to a stand'; the verb can equally mean 'stood his ground', and nothing in the sentence decides between them.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος περὶ τῶν σφόδρα δειλῶν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos peri tōn sphodra deilōn.
sentences.l: The fable is about the exceedingly cowardly.
sentences.n: A closing tag with no verb: περί with the genitive names the sort of man the fable is about, and the 'is' is left to be understood.
